newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-H&M profits jump as stores spread.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-H&M profits jump as stores spread.

text.p: Swedish fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz (H&M) put on another good show for the markets on Thursday, announcing a share split and posting a 44 percent jump in 1995-96 profits as its stores spread across Europe.
The Stockholm-based retailer, which has been one of the hottest stocks on the local bourse over the past year, reported a pre-tax profit of 1.91 billion crowns ($263 million).
Sales in the year ending November 30, 1996, rose 18 percent to 17.21 billion crowns from 14.59 billion crowns a year earlier, a rise of 28 percent excluding currency effects.
"It was a solid report and the result was as expected, showing yet again that H&M is doing a very good job in a quite difficult trading environment," said Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky.
"The company stands out compared to other European retailers."
The market had expected H&M to post a pre-tax profit of 1.85 billion crowns after bouncing back from a relatively weak year in 1995 when trading conditions across Europe were depressed.
H&M, which specialises in competitively priced, high street fashion, has 443 stores across Europe with over 100 in Germany and 117 in Sweden, some of which now sell only underwear and cosmetics.

In 1996 the company added over 50 stores to its list with new investments totalling 700 million crowns. Sales outside Sweden accounted for 76 percent of total group turnover compared with 73 percent in 1995, the company said.
Over the past two months the company's chief executive Stefan Persson, whose father founded the company, has announced plans to open up in France and Finland.
Persson said H&M had already found one store site on the Rue de Rivoli in Paris and negotiations for others were underway. There are plans to open five stores in Finland in the second half of 1997.
"The group will continue to expand strongly in 1997. For the coming year a net addition of around 50 shops is planned," the company said in a statement.
H&M stock has been the fastest mover on the Stockholm bourse over the past year, rising by over 180 percent.
In January 1995 the share price stood at around 386 crowns but by the close of trade on Thursday the share had risen 18 crowns to 1,109 crowns.
Analysts said the stock was the most expensive in nominal prices on the Stockholm bourse, which has triggered some speculation of a share split in recent months.
So it came as no surprise when the company released its annual results that it announced a five-for-one share split.

"I think sentiment-wise this is positive as most shares on the Stockholm bourse are 200-300 crowns so from that point of view it makes sense. But it's nothing that will have an impact on the company's value," a Stockholm-based analyst said.
"For retail clients and private investors it tends to be off-putting to have such a high nominal price on a share, but for institutional investors it really makes no difference."
H&M proposed a dividend of 11 crowns a shares compared with 7.75 crowns in 1994/95. ($1=7.25 crowns)
